claims.text: Arc melting followed by homogenization produces a well-mixed bulk HfNbTaTiZr microstructure.
A comparative HfNbTaTiZr specimen can be prepared with 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed approach integrates ab initio calculations and machine learning to represent structural-defect and oxygen-impurity scattering.
Conventional analytical conductivity predictions for this alloy assume a perfect crystal lattice and omit defect and impurity scattering.
Electron and defect scattering dominate conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr over 0–200 K.
Phonon scattering becomes more pronounced in HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
Impurity effects become more pronounced in HfNbTaTiZr over 300–1200 K.
Dislocations and grain boundaries enhance carrier scattering in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr induces scattering defects or precipitates.
Defect- and oxygen-induced scattering mediates the alloy's conduction behavior.
Accounting for phonon-electron and defect-induced scattering reduces systematic conductivity-prediction error relative to perfect-lattice models.
Machine-learning calibration using data from less-pure samples improves predictive accuracy across both specified temperature regimes.
The defect-aware model will reduce conductivity-prediction error by at least a factor of two relative to a conventional perfect-crystal model over 0–200 K.
The defect-aware model will reduce conductivity-prediction error by at least a factor of two relative to a conventional perfect-crystal model over 300–1200 K.
The predicted accuracy advantage extends to HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The model is expected to apply only over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and at oxygen levels up to approximately 1 wt.% without further calibration.
Applicability at substantially higher impurity levels or outside the stated temperature intervals would require further calibration.
Failure to achieve a factor-of-two error reduction relative to the perfect-crystal model would falsify the hypothesis.
Predictions falling outside experimental uncertainty bounds or failing to capture measured temperature trends would falsify the hypothesis.
